replying_to: Replying to Mechanistic Study of Transformer In-Context Learning with Categorical Outputs
display_title: Official Review of Submission18142 by Reviewer i2U1

summary.value:
This paper investigates in-context learning (ICL) with transformers for categorical outputs.
It shows that categorical targets introduce a nonlinear gradient update that attention-only models cannot represent, revealing a key role for the MLP layers.
The authors further identify conditions where attention-only models still perform well, propose sparse transformer parametrization linked to the functional gradient descent, and validate their theoretical findings through several experiments.

strengths.value: The paper makes theoretical and empirical contributions by focusing on categorical ICL, analyzing the functional gradient descent perspective to explain why MLP layers are necessary for nonlinear expectation updates, and validating these insights through several experiments. So, I think that this paper provide a meaningful findings supported by empirical evidence.

weaknesses.value: While this paper claims that MLPs play a key role in approximating the nonlinear expectation (lines 319–326), this point remains unclear to me from a mathematical perspective.  This may simply be because I have not yet fully understood why the functional gradient descent step is identified with Transformer layers (around line 297). Could you please provide more explanation of the theoretical role of the MLPs ? I elaborate on the specific question below.

questions.value: From a purely theoretical standpoint, if the goal is to approximate the nonlinear mapping $f \mapsto \mathbb{E}(w|f)$, is it truly necessary to rely on MLPs? Couldn’t a single-layer or deep self-attention approximate this mapping as well ?  I have seen recent approximation results (for instance, Hu et al, Universal Approximation with Softmax Attention, 2025; and  Kajitsuka and Sato, Are transformers with one layer self-attention using low-rank weight matrices universal approximators?, 2023; and Furuya et al, Transformers are universal in-context learners, 2024) show that even one-layer or deep attention architectures can achieve universal approximation  without relying on MLPs.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission18142 by Reviewer i2U1

comment.value:
Thank you for your careful review and thoughtful questions. Below we provide answers to your questions.

This paper builds on a line of work that started principally with [vonOswald et al., 2023] and has led to many follow-on studies. This line of work is meant to examine {\em how} a Transformer can do in-context learning. A hypothesis that started with [vonOswald et al., 2023] and has been extended by many is that the Transformer can learn to perform functional gradient descent in its forward pass, and this is how the Transformer can do ICL. However, in almost all of that work, the outcome y_i was real valued, and in that setting it has been shown that {\em each layer} of an attention-only Transformer can perform a step of functional gradient descent. An important recent paper along these lines is [Cheng, et al., 2024]. We note that most of the papers you reference also are assuming real-valued y_i, such as Hu et al, Universal Approximation with Softmax Attention, 2025, and therefore they miss the issue that arises when y_i is categorical.

To answer your question, please look at Eq (5) in the body of the paper. Let's consider what the analogous equation is when y_i is real-valued. When y_i is real, the equation becomes

$\Delta f_{i,\ell}= \frac{\alpha}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N  [y_j −f_{j,\ell}]\kappa (x_i,x_j)$

Notice, it looks similar to Eq (5), but the key thing is that $\Delta f_{i,\ell}$ is now -- for real y_i -- a {\em linear} function of $f_{j,\ell}$. Therefore, there is no nonlinearity of f_{i,\ell} manifested in the update step. In this setting, [Cheng et al. 2024] showed that an attention-only Transformer can perform such functional GD exactly in its forward pass. But critical to this is that y_i is real valued.

When y_i is categorical, we get Eq (5) in our paper, and the term $\mathbb{E}(w|f_{j,\ell})=\mbox{softmax}(W_e^\top f_{j,\ell})$ is now a {\em nonlinear} function of $f_{j,\ell}$. An attention-only model cannot in general implement Eq (5) in a single Transformer layer without approximation, because of the nonlinear $\mathbb{E}(w|f_{j,\ell})$. Therefore, we posit that a role of the MLP layer is to compute the nonlinear   $\mathbb{E}(w|f_{j,\ell})$. None of the prior research that has studied Transformer inference from the standpoint of functional gradient descent has considered the MLP layer, and this is because it is not needed for real y_i. This paper is believed to be the first to consider categorical y_i, which moves us closer to language models, and so doing starts to put a spotlight on a possible important role of the MLP elements in a Transformer (which has not been considered in essentially all of the extensive recent prior work in this research direction, despite the well-known importance of the MLP layers in Transformers).

display_title: Official Review of Submission18142 by Reviewer bQ6R

summary.value: The paper studies the in-context learning of transformers for categorical outputs. Experiments are conducted to show that traditional transformers and attention-only models can indeed learn ICL tasks of categorical outputs. Theoretical analysis is also provided to show that a two-layer attention-only model can perform two steps of GD approximately, but further steps of GD wouldn't be possible without MLP layers.

strengths.value:
1. The paper studies the ICL task of categorical output, which is more relevant to the NLP of transformers where transformers "choose" which token to output.
2. The idea of an attention layer approximating the expectation $\mathbb{E}(w|f)$ through first-order Taylor expansion is somewhat interesting.

weaknesses.value:
1. The writing could be improved. In sec 3, some basic intuition on what the experiments are about could be included at the beginning. The  baselines should also be introduced in a more specific way. For example, I don't understand what the GD model is until I read line 230, which tells me it is a transformer "trained with constraints on its parameters", but the details are left to "the next section". Also, it's a bit strange to call a pretrained transformer model simply by "GD", which may cause some misunderstandings.

2. The conclusions drawn from experiments in sec 3 doesn't seem too surprising, given we already know that transformers can learn classification functions in-context [1,2,3,4].

3. The theoretical derivations in sec 4 largely follows [5] without much novelty, and the conclusioin is that a two layer attention only model can approximate two steps of GD, but further GD steps require MLP layers, which doesn't align with experiments in sec 3. 

4. The experiments in sec 6 doesn't seem to be very relevant to the point of the paper, which is to study the **mechanistic** of TF ICL on categorical data, not **whether** TF can learn the task or not.

[1] Edwards, A., & Camacho-Collados, J. (2024). Language models for text classification: Is in-context learning enough?. arXiv preprint arXiv:2403.17661.

[2] Milios, A., Reddy, S., & Bahdanau, D. (2023). In-context learning for text classification with many labels. arXiv preprint arXiv:2309.10954.

[3] Reddy, G. (2023). The mechanistic basis of data dependence and abrupt learning in an in-context classification task. arXiv preprint arXiv:2312.03002.

[4] Bai, Y., Chen, F., Wang, H., Xiong, C., & Mei, S. (2023). Transformers as statisticians: Provable in-context learning with in-context algorithm selection. Advances in neural information processing systems, 36, 57125-57211.

[5] Wang, A. T., Convertino, W., Cheng, X., Henao, R., & Carin, L. (2024). On Understanding Attention-Based In-Context Learning for Categorical Data. arXiv preprint arXiv:2405.17248.

questions.value:
1. What is the "GD" model and what is its main difference compared with "Trained TF" besides initialization?

2. What is the takeaway message of this paper? The theoretical analysis seems to be inconsistent with the experiments, and the experiments seem to be unsurprising.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission18142 by Reviewer bQ6R

comment.value:
Thank you for your careful review of our paper. Below we address specific comments/questions:

1. We agree that more intuition could be provided earlier as connected to the experiments; we will refine if the paper is accepted, in which we will leverage the additional space. Please note that our notation is standard in the literature, but we realize that not all readers would be aware of that. The "TF" and "GD" notation and terminology was introduced by [vonOswald et al., 2023], and has been widely followed since. 

2. you note "Also, it's a bit strange to call a pretrained transformer model simply by "GD", which may cause some misunderstandings." Actually, the "GD" Transformer is not a pretrained transformer model. On line 230 we write "such that they are sparse in a way connected to functional GD analysis." As noted, this aligns with all prior work in this area of research. We show in Appendix F (in great detail) how the sparsity is manifested as a function of the functional gradient descent perspective. We concede that it may be asking a lot of the reader to examine Appendix F, but it is hard to put all details in the main paper. If you have time, please take a quick look at Appendix F.

3. "The conclusions drawn from experiments in sec 3 doesn't seem too surprising ..." That a Transformer {\em can} perform classification is not surprising. The question is {\em how}. All prior work that has examined Transformer ICL in this class of problems has assumed y_i was real valued, not categorical, and therefore did not consider classification (how it is done). Therefore, all of that prior work did not consider the role of the MLP elements, as when y_i is real valued attention-only Transformers are sufficient. This paper is the first to examine {\em how} the Transformer performs such classification, and in particular the role of the MLP elements, which were not considered in any prior work in the literature on this line of work for mechanistically understanding the Transformer.

4. "The experiments in sec 6 doesn't seem to be very relevant to the point of the paper, ..." We respectively disagree. As you note, a key point of the paper was to understand Transformer inference for categorical observations. We understood this through the lens of functional gradient descent, building in novel ways on prior work. But, as you also noted, it is widely known that Transformers can do classification, so at the end of the day, what impact does analysis like that we have done have for real problems? We show in Section 6 that for real problems (this is a real problem connected to surgery), one does not have sufficient data to train a Transformer ICL classifier from scratch, without restrictions on the model parameters. We demonstrate that one can leverage the highly sparse parameter design for the GD-based Transformer parameters, to solve a real-world problem for which data are limited. So, this experiment answers a key question in the affirmative: The theory connected to functional GD analysis of Transformers can be leveraged for in-context classification in settings for which training data are limited.

5. "What is the "GD" model and what is its main difference compared with "Trained TF"" As noted above, the GD/Trained TF terminology comes from [vonOswald et al., 2023], and has been used widely since. The "GD" model is a Transformer, but one for which the design of the Transformer parameters is aligned with the perspective that the Transformer performs functional gradient descent in its forward pass. This yields highly sparse Transformer parameters (shown in detail in Appendix F). The "Trained TF" Transformer is a standard Transformer, for which the Transformer parameters are learned from scratch, without restriction. One could ask: How do the GD and Trained TF Transformers align, does the Transformer actually learn to perform functional GD in its forward pass, if trained without restrictions? A key take-away from this paper is that yes, the Trained TF model, if trained with enough data, ultimately aligns very well with the GD model. This is not only in terms of predictive accuracy (like in Figs 1 and 2 ), but also in terms of the underlying parameters, as shown in Section 5. 

6. "What is the takeaway message of this paper? The theoretical analysis seems to be inconsistent with the experiments, and the experiments seem to be unsurprising." The theory investigates how a Transformer could perform functional gradient inference on its forward pass, for categorical y_i. The experiments align with the theory, in that a Transformer (without parameter restrictions) does learn to do functional GD (Section 5). While that Transformer {\em can} do classification is unsurprising, {\em how} has been unstudied, and that is what this paper contributes. Also, we show that this theory has practical value, solving a real-world problem (Section 6) that cannot be solved with conventional Transformer technology for classification.

display_title: Official Review of Submission18142 by Reviewer sxQh

summary.value: This paper studies "categorical ICL", a variant of the "ICL for regression setup" of Garg et al in which the labels are categorical rather than real valued. The authors show that an MLP layer can sometimes help in these settings, and suggest that if the training and test distributions match, it may not be as useful to have the MLP. The authors also compare full training with "GD" training, in which some of the weights are constrained in a way that is inspired by the transformers that learn gradient descent to solve regression problems. They demonstrate that this structure often significantly speeds up training. Finally, they demonstrate the effectiveness of GD training on a problem inspired by a medical application.

strengths.value: The application of GD based Transformer training to the real-world problem associated with surgery is very interesting, as is the demonstrated improvement in training speed when using GD training instead of full training.

weaknesses.value:
The model of section 3.1 seems very contrived. Why are the anchor points $\tilde{x}(i)$ needed? Wouldnt it be natural to let $f(x)$ be "anything" (say lipschitz)? Is this just to make the analysis easier or is this fundamental?

Much of the discussion seems very specific to the "Gradient Descent Interpretation" of ICL (Cheng et al). For instance, the discussion around Line 319. How would these discussions extend to more general settings where the objective of the layers is not necessarily to perform gradient descent for a regression problem.

A comparison between full training and GD for the medical task would be useful to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

questions.value:
On line 155, do you mean "... for context $m$"?

It seems like there is a "MLP + attention vs attention-only" and "TF vs GD" comparison in the paper. How are these related? Is the final conclusion that "MLP+attention using GD" is the best when there is a mismatch in training and test distributions, whereas if those distributions match, the MLP is not useful? 

In line 199-204, I think it would be useful to hve a brief description of these datasets. Are they of the form (image, category)? Is the value of C so low to maintain a high N/C ratio?

I think it would be helpful to write out the CA model of Wang et al. for readers who are unfamiliar with it, especially since Figure 3 (left) and (center) agree so well.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission18142 by Reviewer sxQh

comment.value:
Thank you for reviewing our paper, and for your careful attention to the technical content. Below we address specific questions and comments.

Concerning your comments about "anchor points," this is not reflective of assumptions of our model. This is just the way the synthetic data for that experiment was constituted. We followed exactly the setup of [Wang, ICML, 2025], so that we could compare results with that prior work. We repeated their experiment exactly, and the use of "anchor points" was the way they (and hence we) generated the data. What this says is that in this example the latent function used to generate the data (not assumed in or for our model) is manifested by a weighted sum of kernel functions, and the anchor points are just the center positions of the kernels. We underscore, the only assumption we make is that the latent function is differentiable, which connects to the Lipschitz condition you (correctly) note.

"Much of the discussion seems very specific to the "Gradient Descent Interpretation" of ICL (Cheng et al). etc." There is an extensive line of work seeking to understand the forward pass of a Transformer based on examining functional data of the form (x_i,f(x_i)). (Cheng et al.) is an important recent example of that line of work, but it mostly starts and builds upon [vonOswald et al., 2023]. We are following and building on that work. Specifically, in virtually all of that prior work two key assumptions were made: (i)  observations y_i=f(x_i) were deterministic and real-valued, and (ii) attention-only models were considered (the MLP elements of Transformers were not studied). In this paper, a novel consideration is that y_i is categorical, moving beyond real y_i (and closer to language). A key element of this paper is the demonstration that when y_i is categorical, an attention-only model no longer aligns with a functional gradient descent perspective (with each layer performing a functional GD step) -- that perspective was taken in all prior work. The only prior examination of general categorical y_i was [Wang, ICML, 2025]. However, that paper did not consider the Transformer design widely used in these settings (they introduced a cross-attention block), and therefore they also did not study the MLP and its role in this setting.

"A comparison between full training and GD for the medical task would be useful to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method." This, as we note in the paper, is one of the key reasons we developed the GD-based formulation: The fact that the weights are very sparse, and hence the number of unknowns is markedly reduced. In this real-world task, we do not have enough data to train the full Transformer without use of methods like GD, as we have done. Training a Transformer from scratch, without constraint, fails entirely in this setting, because we don't have enough data. This is a real problem, not contrived, and underscores the importance of what we have developed.

"On line 155, do you mean "... for context $m$"?" Yes. Thanks for catching that typo. We will fix it.

"It seems like there is a "MLP + attention vs attention-only" and "TF vs GD" comparison in the paper. ..."  Yes. The terminology "TF" for Trained Transformer (with no restriction on parameters) comes from [vonOswald et al., 2023] and has been used widely in this literature since. Same with the term "GD." So we are following standard notation and terminology. As noted, almost none of the prior work considered the MLP, which was a focus of this submission. Concerning your added comment: We would not say the MLP "is not useful" in the setting you mentioned; we would say it is not {\em needed/required}. We explain in great detail why this is so, both theoretically and empirically, showing that when the training and testing data are matched a linear approximation (no MLP) often works well.

"In line 199-204, I think it would be useful to hve a brief description of these datasets." We agree and we will do as requested in an updated version (accepted papers get one more page, and we will use it for this).

"I think it would be helpful to write out the CA model of Wang et al. for readers ..." We agree. We will do as requested in the updated version of the paper, if accepted. The extra page will be very helpful for this.

display_title: Official Review of Submission18142 by Reviewer 7JG8

summary.value: This paper considers transformer's in-context learning (ICL) ability for categorical outputs. They claim that attention-only transformers are insufficient in this case and the MLP layers in traditional transformers are necessary. They claim they develop a sparse transformer parameterization that trains more efficiently. They also consider ICL in multi-question image analysis in the surgical contexts.

strengths.value: 1. The problem considered is interesting and may potentially deepen our understanding of ICL ability of transformers.

weaknesses.value:
1. The paper is very poorly written. It is very difficult to understand the mains results, both theoretical and empirical. For the empirical results, the experimental setup is described in great detail but not easy to understand. It is unclear what questions they are meant to answer, and why they can answer the questions. There is a list of empirical findings in Section 3.3, but they are not properly discussed and it is unclear if they are well supported by the experiments. For the theoretical analysis, the results are scattered in the informal discussions. It is hard to see what are the main results and their implications, why they are interesting and important. 

2. The claimed sparse transformer parameterization is not properly introduced. 

3. The purpose surgical example is unclear. It seems unrelated to the main theme of the paper other than it is an example of ICL.

display_title: Meta Review of Submission18142 by Area Chair r2T8

summary.value:
Reviewer 7JG8

(1) Clarity is poor, particularly around the sparse transformer parameterization and the surgical example.

Reviewer sxQh

(1) The analysis in Section 3 is "contrived" in the sense that assumptions are not justified or explained in the derivation; (2) How general are the results beyond the "gradient descent interpretation of ICL" from Cheng et al. (2024) is not clear; (3) A proper baseline to ICL is needed on the dataset in GD.

Reviewer bQ6R

(1) Clarity around the experimental setting in Section 3 could be improved; (2) Novelty of the empirical results alone is limited, as classification in-context has been reported in prior work; (3) The theory closely follows Wang et al. (2025); (4) The experiments in Section 6 are insufficiently related to the theory.

Reviewer i2U1

(1) It is not clear how the theory shows that MLPs are needed to approximate the nonlinear statistics of in-context classification.

reviewer_concerns.value:
The authors did not post a response with the appropriate visibility settings, and so I am unable to assess whether concerns would be addressed by a rebuttal.

I will attempt to make my own assessment. Reviewer 7JG8 fails to articulate more than a superficial understanding of the paper, and so I will discount their review. Reviewer i2U1's concern appears to stem from a misunderstanding of the work. However, Reviewer sxQh (1) and Reviewer bQ6R (1; 4) also highlighted some issues in clarity, which I concur with; the submission needs revising, specifically in improving the coherence between the theory and the several experiments, and in differentiating the theoretical result from Wang et al. (2025).

I also concur with Reviewer bQ6R (4) that Section 6 is insufficiently motivated with respect to the contribution of the paper.

reviewer_scores.value: I do not think that the reviewers would upgrade their scores without a major revision of the paper to address the concerns above, and so I cannot recommend acceptance to ICLR 2026.
